notes:
I've gathered verse-by-verse notes for Psalm 136 below. Some limits first. The sources mostly agree on what the psalm means. I found only one real argument between traditions, about election, and only one Reformed-leaning teacher took a side. I found no Orthodox reading and no modern notes from bibleodyssey.org or the NET Bible. Nothing turned up on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching for this psalm, so I've left those out. Enduring Word's page cut off after v. 16, so I don't have David Guzik's comments on vv. 17–26.

**Whole psalm / the refrain**
- It was probably sung responsively in the temple: a priest or Levite called out a reason for praise and the congregation answered with the refrain (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-136/). Guzik notes the same refrain was sung when Solomon dedicated the temple (2 Chronicles 5:13) and when Ezra's temple was dedicated (Ezra 3:11) (same URL).
- The Hebrew word behind "loving devotion" is *hesed*. Guzik says it combines loyalty to a covenant with true love and mercy. He rejects the idea, argued in 1927, that it mainly means "covenant loyalty" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-136/).
- Barnes says the main point is that everything God does, "even though it seemed to be a display of power or of justice, of severity or of wrath," is really mercy (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/psalms/136.htm).
- Matthew Henry says repeating the line 26 times teaches us to notice God's mercy in every single kindness (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/psalms/136.htm).
- Jewish tradition calls it the "Great Hallel" (great psalm of praise). The Jews called it the Great Hallel (= Praise), and it was especially sung at the Passover. (https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-136-his-lovingkindness-everlasting). Constable says it is probably the last of the "Great Hallel" group (Psalms 120–136), though some Jewish scholars counted it alone (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/136-15.html).

**v. 1**
- Barnes: this line matches Psalm 106:1. The Hebrew literally reads "for unto eternity his mercy," meaning it never changes or runs out (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/psalms/136.htm).
- Guzik: God's goodness lies behind everything He is and does. The greatest proof of His lasting mercy is Jesus Christ (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-136/).
- Matthew Henry (Concise) links "mercy" to God's plan to save sinners through Christ (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/136-1.htm).

**vv. 2–3**
- Guzik, quoting G. Campbell Morgan: vv. 1–3 use God's three great names, LORD (*Yahweh*), God (*Elohim*) and Lord (*Adonai*). The phrase may come from Deuteronomy 10:17 (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-136/).
- Wesley: "God of gods" means God is far above anything called a god, whether angels, or princes, or idols (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/psalms/136.htm).
- Barnes: Scripture gives the title "Lord of lords" to Jesus (Revelation 19:16), which shows that He is divine (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/psalms/136.htm).

**v. 4**
- Barnes: the "wonders" are miracles, and all of them serve purposes of mercy (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/psalms/136.htm).
- Augustine (Catholic): the psalm says God "alone" did these wonders because the later ones He did through people and angels (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801136.htm).

**vv. 5–9**
- Guzik: these verses draw on the first four days of creation in Genesis 1. They mean God made the world with His people in mind. Because the psalm moves straight from creation into the Exodus, Guzik argues it treats both as real history (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-136/).
- Barnes: the sun and moon show God's kindness, through daylight and through the stars that guide sailors at night (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/psalms/136.htm).
- Spurgeon's collection on v. 6: the "waters" are the great deep (Genesis 7:11), with the earth's crust spread over them (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps136.cfm).

**v. 10**
- Barnes: killing Egypt's firstborn was mercy to Israel, because Egypt would not otherwise have let them go (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/psalms/136.htm).
- The BibleHub study notes see it as a picture of Christ, the Passover Lamb (https://biblehub.com/study/psalms/136-10.htm).

**vv. 11–12**
- Barnes: "outstretched arm" pictures God putting out His full strength. The phrase echoes Exodus 6:6 and Deuteronomy 4:34 (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/psalms/136.htm).
- A sermon outline in Spurgeon's collection applies v. 11 to God bringing His people out of their old sinful state (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps136.cfm).

**vv. 13–15**
- Guzik, quoting Maclaren: the word "divided" means to hew in two. Israel walked between the halves of the sea as between the halves of a covenant sacrifice (Genesis 15:17) (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-136/).
- v. 15: "swept" literally means "shook off," like a tree shaking off its leaves (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/psalms/136.htm). JFB says it pictures God contemptuously flinging off a reptile (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Psa/Psa_136.cfm).

**v. 16**
- Guzik: the forty years in the wilderness included guidance, food, water, healing and victory, and tested God's mercy severely (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-136/).

**vv. 17–20**
- Barnes: removing wicked kings was a kindness to the world (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/psalms/136.htm).
- Gill: Sihon refused to let Israel pass through and attacked them (Numbers 21:23) (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/136-19.htm).
- Spurgeon's collection applies Og's fall to every later enemy of the church, including Antichrist (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps136.cfm).
- Augustine: when you see what happened to the wicked, make sure it doesn't happen to you (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801135.htm).

**vv. 21–22**
- Matthew Henry: the land was a picture of heaven, "the heavenly Canaan" (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_136.cfm).
- Wesley: Israel is called one "servant" because the people were united in worshipping God (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/psalms/136.htm).

**v. 23**
- Commentators disagree on which "low estate" is meant:
  - The Babylonian exile: JFB, Clarke, the Pulpit Commentary, Coffman (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/136-23.htm; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/136-23.html).
  - Israel's general weakness, when it was few and feeble: Barnes (same URLs).
  - Gill lists the Jewish options: Egypt, the time of the Judges, or Babylon (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/136-23.htm).
- Calvin: the psalmist shows every generation receiving the same goodness as their fathers (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/136-23.html).
- Gill and Spurgeon also apply the verse to a sinner's lost condition before conversion (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/136-23.htm).

**v. 24**
- JFB: "freed" literally means "snatched." It points to the sudden fall of Babylon (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Psa/Psa_136.cfm).
- Spurgeon: we are freed from sin by Christ's blood, from Satan by His power, and from the world by the Holy Spirit (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/136-23.htm).
- Augustine: the rescue was by the Blood of His only-begotten Son (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801136.htm).

**v. 25**
- Wesley: food for all living creatures (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/psalms/136.htm). Barnes reads it the same way and compares Psalm 104:27–28 (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/psalms/136.htm).
- JFB compares Matthew 6:30 (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Psa/Psa_136.cfm).
- Spurgeon's collection: even ordinary blessings all come from grace (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps136.cfm).
- Keil and Delitzsch: the verse looks back to a time when famine came along with slavery (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/136-23.htm).

**v. 26**
- JFB: "God of heaven" appears only once before the exile (Jonah 1:9). Later writers used it to set God apart from idols (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Psa/Psa_136.cfm).
- Barnes: it means the God whose home is heaven. The full measure of His mercy will be our subject of praise forever (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/psalms/136.htm).

**Where Protestant traditions differ**
- **Election (vv. 10–22):** Steven Cole on bible.org argues these verses show God's saving love is a particular love, against those who say God loves everyone equally. He names Dave Hunt as an opponent. God's love was on Israel in a way that it was not on the Egyptians or the Canaanites (https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-136-his-lovingkindness-everlasting). I found no Arminian or Wesleyan reply about this psalm. Wesley's notes don't address the question.
- **Call-and-response in worship:** Barnes, a Presbyterian, warns that the psalm's form shouldn't be used to prove that spoken responses in church services are proper. It may just be a style of Hebrew poetry (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/psalms/136.htm).

**Other views**
- **Catholic (Augustine):**
  - The refrain shows God's mercy is praised above everything else in the psalm (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801136.htm).
  - v. 25: the "food" goes to Gentiles as well as Jews. Augustine links it to Christ's words, "My Flesh is meat indeed" (John 6:55).
  - v. 26: "God of heaven" restates "God of gods." Augustine reads it alongside 1 Corinthians 8:6, "one God… and one Lord Jesus Christ" (same URL).
- **Older scholarship on the date:** Keil and Delitzsch say the language of vv. 23–25 has the stamp of the latest period (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/136-23.htm). Clarke says it was doubtless written after the captivity (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-136.html).
- **Translation:** the NET Bible renders the refrain "his loyal love endures" (https://biblehub.com/p/esv/net/psalms/136.shtml).
